title: Huygens' Principle and Wavefront Propagation
short_intro: Huygens' principle is a geometric construction method used to determine the shape of a wavefront at any subsequent time from its known shape at an earlier time. It postulates that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Geometrical construction of spherical and plane wavefronts, laws of reflection and refraction derived using wave theory, and elementary understanding of secondary wavelets.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Fresnel's modification of Huygens' principle incorporating obliquity factor, Kirchhoff's integral theorem, zone plate analysis, and phase relationships of secondary wavelets.

prerequisites: Phase and amplitude of harmonic waves

concept_notes.heading: Definition of Wavefront
bullets: A wavefront is the locus of all adjacent points in a medium vibrating in the same phase.
The direction of propagation of light (ray) is always perpendicular to the wavefront at any point.
Depending on the source geometry, wavefronts are classified as spherical, cylindrical, or plane.

concept_notes.heading: Huygens' Postulates
bullets: Every point on a given wavefront acts as a secondary source of light, emitting secondary wavelets in all directions with the speed of light in that medium.
The envelope (tangent surface) of these secondary wavelets, considered in the forward direction after a time interval t, defines the new position of the wavefront.
The back-propagation of secondary wavelets is non-existent or has zero amplitude, as accounted for by the obliquity factor.

concept_notes.heading: Laws of Reflection via Wave Theory
bullets: A plane wavefront incident obliquely on a reflecting surface establishes secondary wavelets successively along the boundary.
The time taken by the wave to travel from the incident wavefront to the reflecting surface equals the time taken by the secondary wavelet to travel back.
This equality of distances proves that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r).

concept_notes.heading: Laws of Refraction (Snell's Law) via Wave Theory
bullets: When a plane wavefront crosses the boundary between two optical media of refractive indices n&subscript;1&subscript; and n&subscript;2&subscript;, its speed changes from v&subscript;1&subscript; to v&subscript;2&subscript;.
The secondary wavelets in the second medium travel a distance v&subscript;2&subscript;t in time t, while those in the first medium travel v&subscript;1&subscript;t.
The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction yields the constant refractive index ratio v&subscript;1&subscript;/v&subscript;2&subscript;.

derivations.title: Derivation of the Law of Reflection
derivations.conditions: Plane wavefront incident on a plane reflecting surface at an angle i.
steps: Let a plane wavefront AB be incident on a reflecting surface XY at an angle i.

As point A strikes the surface first, it begins to emit secondary wavelets. By the time point B travels a distance BC = v&subscript;t to reach the surface at C, the secondary wavelet from A has spread out to a radius AD = v&subscript;t.
Drawing a tangent from C to the sphere of radius vt gives the reflected wavefront CD.
In triangles ABC and ADC, angle ABC = angle ADC = 90 degrees, side AC is common, and BC = AD = vt.
Therefore, triangles ABC and ADC are congruent, yielding angle BAC = angle DCA, which proves angle of incidence i equals angle of reflection r.

derivations.title: Derivation of Snell's Law of Refraction
derivations.conditions: Plane wavefront incident on an interface separating two media with speeds v&subscript;1&subscript; and v&subscript;2&subscript;.
steps: Consider a plane wavefront AB incident on the interface XY separating medium 1 (speed v&subscript;1&subscript;) and medium 2 (speed v&subscript;2&subscript;) at angle of incidence i.
When point B reaches the interface at C in time t, distance BC = v&subscript;1&subscript;t.
During this time t, the secondary wavelet originating from A travels a distance AD = v&subscript;2&subscript;t in medium 2.
The refracted wavefront is represented by the tangent CD, making an angle of refraction r with the surface XY, such that angle DCA = r.
From triangle ABC, sin(i) = BC / AC = v&subscript;1&subscript;t / AC. From triangle ADC, sin(r) = AD / AC = v&subscript;2&subscript;t / AC.
Dividing sin(i) by sin(r) gives v&subscript;1&subscript; / v&subscript;2&subscript;, which equals the constant refractive index n&subscript;21&subscript;.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Huygens' Construction of a Plane Wavefront
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parallel wavefronts AB and CD with rays perpendicular to them, showing secondary spherical envelopes advancing in time t.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how a plane wavefront maintains its planar geometry as it propagates through a uniform medium.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual diagrams where candidates identify new wavefront positions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Refraction of a Plane Wavefront at a Boundary
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Incident wavefront AB, boundary XY, refracted wavefront CD, normal lines, and angles i and r clearly marked.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visual proof of wave bending due to altered wave speeds across optical interfaces.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Derivation-based descriptive questions and geometrical optics verification.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spherical Wavefront Propagation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A point source emitting concentric circles representing expanding spherical wavefronts with outward-pointing radial rays.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows intensity diminution with distance following the inverse square law due to expanding spherical surface area (1/r^2).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Multiple choice questions on wavefront geometry and energy spread.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 6000 Å in vacuum enters a medium of refractive index 1.5. Calculate the wavelength of light in the medium.
solution_steps: Identify given values: \lambda_0 = 6000 Å = 6 \times 10^{-7} m, n = 1.5.

solved_numericals.question: A plane wavefront is incident at an angle of 30 degrees on a reflecting surface. What is the angle between the incident wavefront and the reflecting surface?
solution_steps: The angle of incidence i is defined between the incident ray and the normal to the reflecting surface, given as 30 degrees.
The incident wavefront is perpendicular to the incident ray.
The angle between the incident wavefront and the reflecting surface is 90 degrees minus the angle of incidence i.

solved_numericals.question: Monochromatic light of frequency 5 \times 10^{14} Hz passes from air into water of refractive index 4/3. Determine the speed, wavelength, and frequency of the light in water.
solution_steps: Frequency f remains unchanged upon refraction, so f_water = f_air = 5 \times 10^{14} Hz.
Calculate speed in water v = c / n = (3 \times 10^8 m/s) / (4/3) = 2.25 \times 10^8 m/s.
Calculate wavelength in water \lambda_water = v / f = (2.25 \times 10^8 m/s) / (5 \times 10^{14} Hz) = 4.5 \times 10^{-7} m.
solved_numericals.answer: Frequency = 5 \times 10^{14} Hz, Speed = 2.25 \times 10^8 m/s, Wavelength = 4500 Å

assumptions_and_limitations: Huygens' original construction does not explain the absence of backward wavelets; this requires Fresnel's obliquity factor or Kirchhoff's rigorous scalar diffraction theory.
It assumes secondary wavelets have uniform amplitude in all forward directions, which is modified in rigorous diffraction treatments.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Frequency of light changes when it enters a denser medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: Frequency remains constant; only speed and wavelength change.
common_misconceptions.why: Frequency is determined by the source and does not change across material boundaries.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Huygens' wavelets propagate backward with equal intensity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Backward propagation has zero intensity due to phase cancellation and obliquity factors.
common_misconceptions.why: The interference of infinite secondary wavelets causes destructive interference in the reverse direction.

quick_revision: Wavefronts are surfaces of constant phase, always perpendicular to light rays.
Every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets (Huygens' principle).
Snell's law is derived as sin(i)/sin(r) = v_1/v_2 = n_2/n_1.
Frequency remains invariant across media, while wavelength and speed scale inversely with refractive index.
